texto: **Um** + infinitive with **zu** express purpose and usually used when the subject is the same: **Ich fahre mit dem Zug, um Geld zu sparen** (I go by train to save money). The infinitive clause is separated by coma.
If the subject changes, **damit** is usually used with a full sentence: **Er fährt mit dem Zug, damit seine Frau mit dem Auto fahren kann**. **Damit** can also appear with the same subject.

bloques.titulo: damit: for that or with that
texto: As a conjunction, **damit** means «so that» and introduces a subordinate with the verb at the end: **Ich lerne, damit ich die Prüfung bestehe** (study to pass the test). It can also be a pronominal warning with the sense of «with it / with it»: **Damit bin ich einverstanden** (I agree with that). The function and verbal order allow both uses to be distinguished.

opciones.texto: I'm transshipment at the station to take the link train to Munich.

I get off at the station because I've come to my final destination.
opciones.explicacion: «umsteigen» involves continuing to travel in another convoy, not to finish the journey.

bloques.pregunta: Which one is right for «to not miss the train»?

opciones.texto: um den Zug nicht zu verpassen

bloques.frase: Ich nehme ein Taxi, ___ rechtzeitig am Bahnhof anzukommen.

opciones.explicacion: «um ... zu» expresses the purpose with the same grammatical subject.
With infinitive («anzukommen») you cannot use «damit», which requires subject and conjugated verb.
It would mean «without», changing the meaning to «without getting there in time».

intro: Now the purpose: why do we do something. The German has **um … zu** and **damit**.
